spatial_entity.notes: City-node identity only. The account's 'king of Timbuktu' refers to the Songhay askiya in Hunwick's annotation; this entity is neither the Songhay polity nor its territorial extent.

claim.date_text_original: Leo Africanus's Timbuktu description, completed in 1526; possible visit around winter 1509-10, with an alleged second visit around 1512
claim.spatial_precision: Timbuktu city in the textual account; no household, street, market, or practice extent located
claim.summary: Leo Africanus's early-sixteenth-century description of Timbuktu reports enslaved men and women serving townspeople and enslaved women selling provisions. This is one bounded city-level textual tradition for slavery or enslavement, with uncertain visit chronology and disputed eyewitness status.
claim.notes: The 1509-1512 interval is an approximate research window, not four attested annual observations or a continuous practice claim. Hunwick considers personal observation likely; Masonen questions the second visit and whether Leo crossed the Sahara. Pory, Hunwick and Fordham transmit one Leo account, not independent witnesses. Hunwick renders captive sale 'in Timbuktu' (p. 281), Pory says 'unto the merchants of Tombuto' (pp. 287-288), and Fordham says 'in the market at Timbuktu'. Preserve that location variance as a separate trade lead; do not assert a physical Timbuktu market or add a formal network facet from this packet. No population share, intensity, chattel/property status, polity-wide generalization, or continuity is inferred.

territorial_practice.notes: Classifies the reported city-level presence of enslaved residents and service only. P-level, prevalence, duration, precise place of sale, and Songhay territorial practice remain unassigned.
